newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - New markets glitter in miners' eyes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New markets glitter in miners' eyes.

text.p: Political changes across the globe combined with pressure to discover new mineral wealth lies behind a recent exploration boom.
The world's big mining houses and hundreds of smaller companies have poured increasing resources into newly-accessible emerging markets in a hunt for gold, copper, nickel and other minerals.

"Only a few years ago, most of the countries of Latin America, Africa, the Soviet bloc, China and southeast Asia were either not permitting foreign exploitation of their mineral reserves or had placed impossible hurdles in the way," analyst David Williamson told a conference on emerging markets.
"Now all that has changed, albeit slowly in some countries, and exploration and mining development can now take place almost anywhere," he added.
A CHANGING POLITICAL AND MINING CLIMATE
Since 1991, spending on mining exploration has doubled to an estimated $3.5 billion last year, and is likely to increase this year to $4-$5 billion, says Canada-based Yorkton Securities Inc.
The biggest explosion of growth has been in emerging markets, with annual exploration spending in Latin America swelling to $800 million from $140 million over five years.
These are followed by African countries such as Ghana, Indonesia in southeast Asia and the former Soviet republics of Russia, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, analysts say.
A combination of factors has fuelled the boom.

--Emerging markets open their doors. In Latin America, copper-rich Chile led the way to woo foreign investors to bring money and modern mining practices to underdeveloped deposits. Others have followed to reform mining and foreign exchange laws.
The break-up of the Soviet Union and China's emergence have also opened the possibility of huge, uncharted deposits.

--Stunning finds. Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd shot from an unknown penny stock to the big league with the discovery of the spectacular Busang gold deposit in Indonesia. Such finds spur other miners to seek out their own El Dorado.

--Environmental pressure. Mining is a messy business and a heightened concern in developed countries about environmental damage means lengthy studies -- and delays. Emerging markets eager to augment their struggling economies are less choosy.

--Investment climate. Strong capital markets in recent years have armed hundreds of junior companies, mostly Canadian, with cash and a dream. Institutional investors buy shares of the juniors, hoping they will strike it rich or be bought out by a major producer to boost the share price.
GOLD REIGNS SUPREME
Gold still dazzles investors and miners and remains the goal of most exploration efforts, with copper and nickel rating a distant second and third, analysts say.
Emerging markets are soon expected to overtake the powerhouses of gold production -- South Africa, the United States, Canada and Australia -- in terms of gold output.

"It would seem likely that in the next five years, the big four will lose their special status held for nearly 150 years of producing more than half the world's annual production," Stewart Murray, chief executive of Gold Fields Mineral Services, told a gold conference in Istanbul.
Existing big mining houses, however, are likely to remain the leaders in the industry, he added.
One of the world's top three gold producers, Canada's Barrick Gold Corp., says it intends to double in size over the next decade, in part through expansion into South America.

South Africa, while still by far the world's biggest gold producer, is plagued by declining output. Last year it produced just 23 percent of the world's output of gold, but 25 years ago its share was nearly 70 percent, a Gold Fields analyst said.

Some of country's gold miners are taking action to ensure they are not left behind. South African mining giant Gencor has slated 80 percent of its exploration budget outside South Africa. A decade ago, that figure was just five percent.
RISKS REMAIN IN EMERGING MARKETS
The trade-off for forging into potentially lucrative but unfamiliar territory is greater risk, from coup d'etat to misunderstandings over international mining practices.
Big Canadian producer Placer Dome has been trying for months to get a $35 million deposit back from Kazakhstan, after deciding to pull out of a project in the former Soviet republic.
"They've been stalling and have not given us satisfactory response to our agreement," said company spokesman Hugh Leggatt.
"There needs to be an improved understanding at the government level of how free markets work. You don't do business the way they chose to do it."

Bre-X is mired in an ownership dispute over the Busang deposit with one of its Indonesian partners. Its stocks have taken a beating since the dispute was announced this month, and the Indonesian government has delayed contracts of work for the property until problems are resolved.
Canada-based Sherritt International has faced a U.S. black list since entering a joint agreement with a state nickel producer in Cuba, the target of U.S. sanctions.
The rush of investment dollars may also have started to plateau recently as the equity markets peak at all-time highs.

"Now only the best junior mining companies are going to survive," said emerging markets analyst Rajat Kohli. "But we haven't seen the end of it -- we still have India and China and Central Asia in the former Soviet Union."
